content:
INDUSTRY ANALYSIS: How an opportunity now presents itself to rethink the wine equalisation tax and its accompanying rebate system

The way of taxing wine in Australia is imperfect. With the termination, recently, of the Wine Tourism and Cellar Door grants, wine historian Edward Cavanagh provides an overview of recent policy developments in order to call into question the current system of bundling together a wholesale tax and a goods and services tax with rebates.

 

In the recent federal budget of May 2026, it was announced by the Labor government that the Wine Tourism and Cellar Door grant was winding up.

The decision has taken many within the industry by surprise.

A sense of surprise is fairly enough felt.

After all, just a few weeks earlier, the very same initiative was being flaunted by the government as an example – indeed, the foundational example – of the work it is doing to ‘focus on growing domestic demand by encouraging visitors to wine’. These are the remarks published in the official government response of April 2026 to a Senate Committee report of 2025 on the grape and wine sector. Treasurer Jim Chalmers must have missed it in his inbox.

Australian Grape & Wine is understandably livid.

“At the worst possible time,” writes CEO Lee McLean in a press release, “this Government has chosen to withdraw a program that directly supports regional businesses.” He continues: “For many producers, this [grant] is essential to maintaining cashflow and profitability. Ending it now effectively pulls the rug out from under businesses already facing enormous pressure.”¹

This article will examine the merits and policy history of the grant in question in order to establish the necessary background to an argument I will make: namely, that its abolition presents an important opportunity.

Now, I think, is the time for the industry to rethink its blasé acceptance of the ways in which grants, rebates and taxes have applied to cellar door operations and winery businesses across Australia. And this requires a new spirit of criticism towards the wine equalisation tax (WET).

In an attempt to inspire that, this article will present a chronological account of how we got to this point in order to set out what might lay ahead in the future.

 

How did we get here?

Despite the promise of Bob Hawke’s treasurer, Paul Keating, in August of 1983, that no tax would be imposed on table wines by the Australian Labor Party in the run-up to the budget, an ad valorem (i.e., value-calculated) wholesale tax on wine was introduced in 1984 at 10 per cent.

Up and up, under Labor, it went: to 20 per cent in 1986, then to 26 per cent in 1991, and then to 31 per cent in 1993. Under the coalition, it went up further still: to 41 per cent in 1999.

By this time, John Howard and Peter Costello were preparing to introduce a broad-based Goods and Services Tax (GST) of 10 per cent. Even if the GST became less and less broad as a result of exceptions carved out in the Senate, it is important only to point out that wine was not exempted from GST.

In order to achieve roughly the same amount of total tax revenue from domestic wine sales, the government introduced an additional Wine Equalisation Tax (or, the WET). Calculated at 29 per cent, the WET in addition to the 10 per cent GST sequentially approximates to the same rate that had been applied through the wholesale tax of 41 per cent.

Such a high rate of taxation applying ad valorem (rather than volumetrically calculated) rewarded producers (and consumers) of cheap bottles with a lower tax burden while punishing producers (and consumers) of expensive ones with a higher tax burden. Among other things, this utterly contradicted the cult of premiumisation that was taking off at this period, since the WET indirectly incentivised the mass production of cheap wine.

The principal curiosity of the WET system is that it has never been allowed to operate puristically. For no sooner had the law come in and replaced the wholesale sales tax than a 14 per cent rebate was provided for cellar door and mail order sales up to a wholesale value of $300,000 per annum.

It instilled confidence in nobody that the Howard government had got the initial rate of tax correct in the first place when the same government immediately saw a need to introduce a system for assistance to help out the smaller-scale boutique winery operations to whom it was now thought an unfair proportion of tax applied to their sales. But even if this rebate, which replaced and centralised some of the older state-level subsidies, was justified in the interests of sustaining a growing wine tourism sector – since sales generated at the farmgate were considered, on the whole, good for regional economies – it was a bad omen for the tax that it felt unfair from the very outset, and required a system of offsets for it be seen to operate equitably.

In 2004, the cellar door rebate was replaced by a similar initiative known as the WET rebate, which allowed producers to claim a full offset of the WET they paid on wine whether it was sold at the farmgate or not. In a move that continued to be defended for the benefits that it brought to ‘rural and regional Australia’, producers were henceforth able to claim 29 per cent of the price sold at what was meant to be the last wholesale price, subject to a limit of $290,000 per financial year. This essentially allowed eligible producers to sell $1 million worth of wine before paying any WET.

And the jackpot just kept on climbing. Introduced in a federal budgetary context that was characterised by moderately low confidence in the short-term future of the Australian wine industry, the effective tax-free threshold was lifted to $1.7 million from 1 July 2006, when the maximum WET rebate was increased to $500,000.

Over the next decade, as the system was inefficiently administered by the ATO without proper guidance, it came to be rorted in extraordinary ways. Multiple rebates were claimed on the same wine. Grapegrowers used imaginative contracts and ‘quoting’ systems to claim it for themselves. Winery operations bought and sold among themselves and often split into multiple entities to maximise their rebates. Wholesalers, brokers, and retailers adopted pricing strategies to manipulate prices in their favour, and even claimed the rebate for their own in-house brands. Probably most surprising of all, winery businesses in New Zealand even claimed eligibility for it.

As for the original intended rebate recipients – small businesses in regional Australia with struggling cellar doors – the rebates became a lifeline that were factored into every single business model across the country. However, the conclusion cannot be avoided that the rebate became responsible for propping up a number of unviable and often unserious small winery businesses in Australia during a prolonged period of downturn and glut.

The Winemakers’ Federation of Australia acknowledged some of these rorts, but closed its eyes to others. With some of its more influential members wishing to retain the ad valorem tax model, many of them paying accountants who were experts in the manipulation of tax law, the WFA could never afford to go the whole hog on the issue. But it did, in these years, what it could: claiming that the rebate system was adding to the ‘wine glut’ by encouraging producers of unprofitable wine. After the Henry Tax Review (2009) was delivered to the Labor government, which made a compelling case for a lowest-possible volumetric exaction of tax on wine sales to replace the ad valorem WET system and the accompanying rebate, the WFA became strongly opposed to the introduction of a volumetric wine tax, and it was successful in holding this line persistently and persuasively at every opportunity; on this position, they were supported by the Wine Grape Growers’ Council of Australia, who held the same position from 2010 onwards.

As late as 2016, however, a WFA media release could confirm: ‘The Federation does not have a policy on how the WET tax should be calculated’. This strikes me as remarkable, given how important this policy was to the sector, but probably speaks somewhat to the difficulty of harmonising the differing views of members.

After some of the rebate loopholes had become exposed, they captured the attention of Malcolm Turnbull and Scott Morrison.

In 2017, some (but far from all) of these loopholes were closed by amendments to the legislation, which saw eligibility criteria tightened up, and the WET producer rebate cap reduced from $500,000 to $350,000.

To sweeten the deal, the government introduced a new grant system to provide an additional $10 million annually through a Wine Tourism and Cellar Door Grant for any eligible producers who were set to max out on the newly constricted $350,000 WET rebate allocation. This was thought to be a temporary but fair measure to allow companies the opportunity to reconfigure and adapt to the new and less generous rebate.

Effectively this provided anywhere between $1 and $100,000, in addition to the $350,000 WET rebate, for businesses with rebatable domestic cellar door sales in the country through a Commonwealth grant program that was not directly hypothecated from the WET. Instead, legislation had to be amended to provide Wine Australia with responsibility for administering and delivering the cellar door grant.

This was designed to be a temporary initiative. But a cynical political calculation was made that it could be extended and re-announced to great political fanfare after every round or two, which was a gift not just for the coalition, but also, after 2022, for the Labor government.

Instead of reducing the rebate to $290,000, which was the original intention of the 2017 reforms, the Albanese government announced in February last year that the rebate would rise to $400,000. Here was the clearest signal since Kevin Rudd and Wayne Swan that the idea of inefficiently refunding a portion of tax to recipients regardless of means or deservedness retains bipartisan support at the Commonwealth level.

Recall, however, that the reduction of the $500,000 cap was accompanied by the introduction of a special fund for eligible producers who were set to max out at $350,000. The Wine Tourism and Cellar Door grant program provided additional top ups to the WET rebate for legitimately operating cellar doors, and effectively shared around a portion of money ($10 million per year or ‘round’) to qualifying applicants (up to $100,000 per business).

After it was re-announced both by Morrison and by Albanese in gestures more to the electorate than to the industry, Chalmers and Albanese thought better of it after the recent election.

 

Where do we go now?

While it certainly feels possible that the Labor government is waiting for a more electorally opportune moment to resurrect it or introduce some other kind of subsidy for the boutique side of the sector, there is every possibility that the grant is gone for good.

WET reform, too, is also off the cards. Even if this had been a recommendation offered in the Emerson Review (2025), the government clarified that this recommendation was ‘noted’ in its official response, which basically means ‘not interested’.

So the grant is gone, but we are stuck with the rebate.

My position is that the rebate should never have existed in the first place; its roll-out was only justifiable, and regrettable, because the WET rate was calculated too highly (and also, arguably, on the wrong metric). If a rebate was necessary, it should only have existed for as long as it took the government to get around to reducing, reforming, and simplifying the wholesale tax rate on wine. As soon as it had become clear that the rebate was not a temporary mechanism – that is, when Swan nodded it through for another year and Rudd allowed it to stay on the books – there was an obvious way for that government, and if not that government then any one of its two or three successors, to fix the rebate eligibility issue. But instead of devising a simple way through legislation to limit the payouts to the original intended recipients of it – small regional businesses with cellar doors, many of whom were so close to insolvency that many of them became dependent on the rebate for very survival – instead, what the ATO saw, and what the existing tax law did little to prevent, was an expansive and broad number of recipient entities emerging to claim the rebate.

And the administration alone of the scheme is expensive, costing the ATO a fortune just to process and pay out the rebates.

Despite changes to the legislation in 2017, the WET remains as imperfectly calculated today as it was when it was first introduced.

For starters, it is inordinately complex. If it is right for smart economists to aspire for any country’s tax policy to be simple enough for it to go onto two A4 pages, then the model of applying taxation to wine should take no more than three sentences, and probably needs only two: the second one reading ‘no rebates, no workarounds, no thresholds, no grants’.

Any tax that requires a system of grants and rebates to be seen to operate fairly is a tax that is not fit for purpose.

And I do not adopt that cliché without substance: it is right to consider the purpose of a wholesale tax on wine.

Ken Henry did this in 2009, so we really don’t have to today.

Taxes on alcohol outside of the GST carry little rationale unless they are hypothecated to address the ‘spillover costs’ of alcohol abuse in society, Henry powerfully claimed. Henry was also convincing in his argument that a volumetric tax on alcohol is favourable over an ad valorem tax because it disincentivises the over-consumption of higher volumes of cheap wine and nudges drinkers towards smaller sips of premium wines. This is also squarely in keeping with an ascendant health-conscious belief, held by governments and the anti-alcohol lobby alike, that everybody should just be drinking less and living forever. To look at this another way, if it’s unrealistic that Australians are ever going to be implored by the government or Wine Australia to drink more and die younger, then it’s reasonable at least to hope that Australians will be incentivised to buy wisely in a product category that is sustainable, competitive, healthy and manageable. More to the point, such a tax would bring the prices of premium wines down, while indirectly encouraging higher quality standards and competition in that bracket.

Although Henry is unlikely to approve of the suggestion, the argument could also be made that a variable tax rate on wine could apply to different types of entities in order to correct problems of market concentration that have not been corrected in other parts of the law, although I admit this would make things complicated. Still, if grants and rebates have been justified time and again on the basis of supporting regional tourism and cellar door operators, then the same logic should more suitably apply to an argument for lower tax burdens at the point of sale for cellar door operators in certain if not all wine regions, rather than using slap-dash rebates. This method would be cheaper and more effectively targeted.

WET reform needs to come back onto the agenda. The rate of taxation needs to come down. The rebates and grants need to go. And if we really are to persevere with an ad valorem calculation, a strong case needs to be made for its universal retention in 2026: a case more sophisticated than simply a glib admission that this is the way we have become used to taxing wine in Australia.

References

¹Australian Grape & Wine, Media Release: ‘Budget reveals continued Government inaction as wine industry crisis deepens’ (12 May 2026).

title: Vintessential by Winechek achieves international standard accreditation ISO 17034
summary:
Vintessential by Winechek has achieved ISO 17034 accreditation for the standards of its test kits. Vintessential explained that certified reference material (CRM) represents a significant change from non-accredited standards. It is a standard that has undergone rigorous testing to make sure the sample is homogeneous and stable, according to the company. The standard is also tested under “traceable lab conditions”.

content:
Vintessential by Winechek has achieved ISO 17034 accreditation for the standards of its test kits.

Vintessential explained that certified reference material (CRM) represents a significant change from non-accredited standards. It is a standard that has undergone rigorous testing to make sure the sample is homogeneous and stable, according to the company. The standard is also tested under “traceable lab conditions”.

Now a requirement for many laboratories that are accredited to ISO 17025, these are the first CRM manufactured and readily available in Australia for Ethanol (NIR), Glucose/Fructose, L-malic acid, Acetic acid, Sucrose and citric acid. Vintessential said that until recently, CRM often had extended shipping times and were extremely expensive.

Dr Carly Gamble and Dr Victoria Hughes explained to Daily Wine News what this achievement means and why it is important for winemakers in Australia.

“ISO 17034 is the international standard that specifies the competence requirements for reference material producers (RMPs). It ensures that reference materials are produced using scientifically sound methods and are fit for their intended purpose,” the pair began.

“For winery laboratories, using ISO 17034 accredited Vintessential reference material provides confidence that analytical results are accurate, traceable and reliable. Unlike general quality standards, ISO 17034 focuses specifically on the production of reference materials used to calibrate instruments, validate analytical methods and verify laboratory performance.

“ISO 17034 accreditation allows us to provide certificates of analysis with our standards as certified reference materials.”

Moreover, the two shared that using accredited Vintessential reference materials reduces the risk of incorrect calibration, method bias, failed proficiency testing, non-conforming laboratory audits and incorrect product release decisions.

As for what drove the decision to pursue accreditation, the duo said it was motivated by market need.

“We were receiving more and more enquires from our customers for traceability documentation that really made this accreditation a natural progression of the continued optimisation of our manufacturing department.

“The products are so unique in the reference material space that the process was more complicated than we initially thought, saying that, having ISO 17025 accreditation for the testing and calibration needed to validate the standards definitely worked in our favour,” Gamble and Hughes said.

They believe the accreditation has international significance and positions the Australian company as “world leaders in quality control”.

“Australia is now home to one of only a handful of reference material producers specifically addressing wine science. Our customers want to produce world class wines and having world class analysis behind the winemakers is the perfect combination.”

Winechek Pty Ltd, who own and manufacture the Vintessential test kit brand, operate laboratories in Margaret River WA, Barossa Valley SA and Yarra Valley VIC, which are accredited under ISO 17025. Winechek produce the Vintessential test kits and reference materials in its own manufacturing department in the Yarra Valley.

Their message for wineries who are not yet using certified reference standards in their laboratory programs is simple, “don’t be intimidated by quality control”.

“We have over 20 years’ experience in QC (quality control) and testing in wine and beverage science, reach out to us for more information on how we can assist in your QC programs,” the pair said.

title: Punt Road Wines and Richmond Football Club launch limited-release wine collaboration
summary:
Punt Road Wines and Richmond Football Club have launched ‘The Home Ground’, a limited-release 2025 Cabernet Shiraz and the first wine in a new collector series created by the two partners. Only 1,885 individually numbered bottles have been produced, marking Richmond Football Club’s founding year and bringing together “two histories with roots on Melbourne’s Punt Road”. The wine is available to Richmond members first from Monday 17 August and will release to the public on Saturday 22 August. Punt Road Wines explained it takes its name from the original Airlie Bank vineyard planted on Punt Road in the 1850s, near the ground Richmond would later call home. Today, the Napoleone family grows and makes wine at its Coldstream estate in the Yarra Valley, which the family has farmed since 1948.

The post Punt Road Wines and Richmond Football Club launch limited-release wine collaboration appeared first on Winetitles.
content:
Jarrod Johnson and Shane Dunne. Image supplied

Punt Road Wines and Richmond Football Club have launched ‘The Home Ground’, a limited-release 2025 Cabernet Shiraz and the first wine in a new collector series created by the two partners.

Only 1,885 individually numbered bottles have been produced, marking Richmond Football Club’s founding year and bringing together “two histories with roots on Melbourne’s Punt Road”.

The wine is available to Richmond members first from Monday 17 August and will release to the public on Saturday 22 August.

Punt Road Wines explained it takes its name from the original Airlie Bank vineyard planted on Punt Road in the 1850s, near the ground Richmond would later call home. Today, the Napoleone family grows and makes wine at its Coldstream estate in the Yarra Valley, which the family has farmed since 1948.

The Home Ground is made entirely from fruit grown on the Napoleone Vineyard in Coldstream. A blend of 67% Cabernet Sauvignon and 33% Shiraz, the 2025 wine is “dark fruited and perfumed, with notes of liquorice, earth and spice and the depth to reward cellaring for 15+ years”.

A small number of one-of-a-kind collector bottles have also been signed by Richmond players, with selected bottle numbers matching each player’s guernsey number. These will be available in individual gift boxes, limited to one per customer.

title: “The wines are just getting better” in the Hunter Valley
summary:
Last Friday, 16 Hunter Valley producers were celebrated with trophies at the 2026 PKF Hunter Valley Wine Show luncheon at Oaks Cypress Lakes Resort. The 54th show featured 69 exhibitors and 652 entries, judged over three days at Singleton Showground, assisted by the School of Infantry and led by a panel chaired by Toni Paterson MW. Merrick Watts hosted the luncheon as master of ceremonies and Dr Jamie Goode from the UK was welcomed as international judge. “The Hunter Valley has this beautiful historical thread, and its location is quite unique, so when you come here and taste the wines you discover this place is producing some fantastic wines,” said Goode. Returning for her second year as chair, Toni Paterson said her main takeaway was that the wines are “just getting better”.

content:
The winners at the 2026 Hunter Valley Wine Show. Image supplied

Last Friday, 16 Hunter Valley producers were celebrated with trophies at the 2026 PKF Hunter Valley Wine Show luncheon at Oaks Cypress Lakes Resort.

The 54th show featured 69 exhibitors and 652 entries, judged over three days at Singleton Showground, assisted by the School of Infantry and led by a panel chaired by Toni Paterson MW. Merrick Watts hosted the luncheon as master of ceremonies and Dr Jamie Goode from the UK was welcomed as international judge.

“The Hunter Valley has this beautiful historical thread, and its location is quite unique, so when you come here and taste the wines you discover this place is producing some fantastic wines,” said Goode.

“I was most impressed by the Shiraz. The focus, precision and age worthiness of the Shiraz brackets are quite unlike anything else in Australia.

“These wines would sit well in any contemporary red line up from around the world. That was probably the most exciting element for me.”

The Doug Seabrook Memorial Trophy for Best Red Wine of Show was awarded to De Iuliis Wines for its 2023 Limited Release Shiraz, which also received the Hector Tulloch Memorial Trophy for Best Shiraz and the James Busby Memorial Trophy for Best Three-Year-Old and Older Shiraz.

The Thomas Wines 2024 Sweetwater Ridge Shiraz was awarded the Len Evans Trophy for Best Single Vineyard Red Wine, as well as the Stibbard-Hulin Trophy for Best Two-Year Old Shiraz. Best Current Vintage and One-Year Old Shiraz, the Alexander Munro Memorial Trophy, was also awarded to Thomas Wines for their 2025 Synergy Shiraz.

Best Museum Red Wine and John Lewis Trophy was awarded to Mount Pleasant Wines for their 2018 Rosehill 1965 Vines Shiraz.

Mercer Wines took the Maurice O’Shea Memorial Trophy for Best Other Red Varietal for their 2025 Limited Release Shiraz, Pinot Noir.

Returning for her second year as chair, Toni Paterson said her main takeaway was that the wines are “just getting better”.

“You see such evolution in the wines of the Hunter Valley at the moment, with people actively trying different things to produce better and charming wines that the market is demanding,” she said.

After judging the Semillon classes, Paterson commented that “Hunter semillon has never been better at traversing the ability to be enjoyed young but also have ageing potential”.

The Petrie-Drinan Trophy for Best White Wine of Show was awarded to Brokenwood Wines for their 2019 ILR Reserve Semillon, which also won the Len Evans Trophy for Best Single Vineyard White Wine, Drayton Family Trophy for Best Semillon and McGuigan Family Trophy for Best Two-Year Old and Older Semillon. The Marshall-Flannery Trophy for Best Current Semillon was also awarded to Brokenwood for their 2026 Oakey Creek Vineyard Stockyards Block Semillon and the Karl Stockhausen Trophy for Best One-Year-Old Semillon to Margan Family Wines for its 2025 Fordwich Hill Semillon.

The Tyrrell Family Trophy for Best Museum White Wine was awarded to Tyrrell’s for their 2013 Belford Semillon.

Audrey Wilkinson was awarded the Iain Riggs Wine of Provenance for the second consecutive year for their 2026, 2017 and 2013 Winemakers Selection Semillon.

Goode noted that a highlight for him was the Chardonnays, “which do really well in the Hunter Valley”.

The Murray Tyrrell Chardonnay Trophy was awarded to Silkman Wines for their 2025 Silk Chardonnay, also winning the George Wyndham Memorial Trophy for Best Current and One-Year Old Chardonnay. Silkman Wines collected all three Chardonnay trophies, also being awarded the Henry John Lindeman Memorial Trophy for Best Two-Year old and older Chardonnay for their 2023 Silk Chardonnay.

The Kaloudah Trophy for Best Wine from a Small Producer was awarded to Bonvilla Estate for their 2026 Single Vineyard Semillon.

Trophies were also awarded for Best Rose to McLeish Estate for their 2026 Dwyer Rose Merlot, to Hungerford Hill for Best Verdelho for their 2026 Verdelho, to Briar Ridge for Best Other White Varietal & White Blends for their 2026 Limited Release Albarino, to Glenesk Wines for their Wiley Rooster 2025 Late Harvest Semillon and to Draytons Family Wines for their NV Balthasar Liqueur Verdelho for Best Fortified Wine or Vermouth.

Mount Eyre was awarded the Lone Pine Barracks Officers Mess Silver Bullet for their Nero 2025 Nero D’Avola.

Alongside the Wine Trophies, two industry scholarships were presented. The 2026 Tyrrell Family Advanced Viticulture Scholarship was awarded to Jeremy O’Brien of Davis Family Group, and the 2026 Alasdair Sutherland Scholarship to Michael Wells of Usher Tinkler Wines and Thea Wines.

The Hunter Valley’s reputation is built by the people who choose to stay and build their careers here,” said Jennie Curran, CEO of the Hunter Valley Wine & Tourism Association.

“Jeremy and Michael represent the next generation who will carry that forward.”

title: De Bortoli expands Ancient Soils range with new Grenache
summary:

content:
The Grenache release follows the earlier success of the Ancient Soils Tempranillo Touriga. Image supplied

De Bortoli Wines has added a Grenache to its Ancient Soils range, “continuing its exploration of Heathcote’s remarkable ancient Cambrian soils”.

Located in Northern Heathcote near Corop, the De Bortoli family’s Freemans Bridge (75ha) and Taylors (15ha) vineyards are planted on deep Cambrian red soils over limestone. Formed more than 500 million years ago, the winery explained that these ancient soils are among the oldest winegrowing soils on Earth, producing wines of depth, purity and structure.

Ancient Soils Grenache is grown in these conditions, “thriving in the warm climate and expressing the distinctive character of the site”.

Chief winemaker Steve Webber said the Grenache showcases a different side of Heathcote.

“With Ancient Soils Grenache, we’re really leaning into making a wine that represents Heathcote. It’s a very fruit-driven style of wine, but there’s a lot of really well-matured tannin in it, which I think is a hallmark of Grenache from the region. We work really hard to harness those natural grape tannins without extracting too hard. I think the wine brings fragrance, energy and texture while still carrying the structure and sense of place that define Heathcote,” Webber said.

Ancient Soils Grenache was fermented in clay amphora, concrete and stainless-steel vats, with skin contact ranging between 20 and 30 days. 10 per cent whole bunch was included across the blend with intermittent pump-overs and plunging before the wine was matured in stainless steel and concrete ahead of bottling in autumn 2026, according to De Bortoli.

Described as “medium-bodied and vibrant”, the winery said Ancient Soils Grenache “offers perfumed red and blue fruits, wet stone and sweet spice”.

“Elegant and lively, it is fresh, focused and finely structured, with compact lingering tannins, gentle acidity and a seamless finish,” the company said.

The Grenache follows the release of the Ancient Soils Tempranillo Touriga.

title: Y Series launches limited-edition NFL collection with prizes up for grabs
summary:
Y Series has announced a limited-edition NFL collection to celebrate the first-ever regular season game of NFL in Australia and to offer fans the chance to win a trip to the Super Bowl LXI in Los Angeles. The limited-edition collection features NFL-inspired packaging across “some of Y Series’ most popular varietals” including Prosecco, Pinot Grigio, Lighter Pinot Grigio, Sauvignon Blanc, Riesling, Pinot Noir and Shiraz. CEO of Hill-Smith Family Estates Karl Martin said the NFL game in Melbourne this September 11 presents a unique opportunity for Y Series to be part of one of the year's biggest cultural and sporting moments. Moreover, Y Series shared that from 1 August to 31 December 2026, purchasing any Y Series wines from Dan Murphy’s or BWS allows customers to enter the draw for the chance to win a trip for two to Super Bowl LXI in Los Angeles. 100 instant-win NFL Shop Australia vouchers are also up for grabs valued at $100 each.

content:
Customers can purchase the limited-edition collection from Dan Murphy’s or BWS for the chance to win a trip to the Super Bowl LXI. Image supplied

Y Series has announced a limited-edition NFL collection to celebrate the first-ever regular season game of NFL in Australia and to offer fans the chance to win a trip to the Super Bowl LXI in Los Angeles.

The limited-edition collection features NFL-inspired packaging across “some of Y Series’ most popular varietals” including Prosecco, Pinot Grigio, Lighter Pinot Grigio, Sauvignon Blanc, Riesling, Pinot Noir and Shiraz.

CEO of Hill-Smith Family Estates Karl Martin said the NFL game in Melbourne this September 11 presents a unique opportunity for Y Series to be part of one of the year’s biggest cultural and sporting moments.

“The NFL Melbourne Game coming to Australia is a huge moment for sports fans, and we’re proud that Y Series will be part of how people celebrate it.

“Whether it’s gathering friends for a watch party, heading to Melbourne for the game or simply enjoying the atmosphere surrounding the event, this partnership is about creating memorable moments and giving fans another way to connect with the excitement. That’s exactly the sort of occasion Y Series was made for,” Martin said.

Y Series will also be offering limited-edition Y Series cans for fans to enjoy at the Melbourne Cricket Ground (MCG) on game day as well as at the 3-day NFL Kickoff Festival in Melbourne Park.

Moreover, Y Series shared that from 1 August to 31 December 2026, purchasing any Y Series wines from Dan Murphy’s or BWS allows customers to enter the draw for the chance to win a trip for two to Super Bowl LXI in Los Angeles. 100 instant-win NFL Shop Australia vouchers are also up for grabs valued at $100 each.

Charlotte Offord, NFL general manager – Australia and New Zealand, said partnerships like Y Series help bring the NFL experience closer to Australian fans.

“The NFL’s presence in Australia continues to grow, and partnerships like Y Series play an important role in helping us create meaningful local experiences for our fans. Together, we’re giving Australians more ways to connect with the game and be part of the excitement surrounding the NFL Melbourne Game and beyond.”

The range will be available nationally from September through Dan Murphy’s, BWS, Liquorland and independent retailers with a RRP of $15.

content:

Burnside Village ambassador and acclaimed wine writer Nick Ryan is set to host an “immersive food and wine masterclass” at Eccoci Ristorante this Wednesday to answer the question, “what happens when Italy’s most celebrated grape varieties meet their Australian counterparts at the same table?”.

The event, titled La Grande Tavola, will feature a five-course degustation, with each course presenting an Italian wine from its grape variety’s home region alongside an Australian wine of that same grape, inviting guests “to taste how place, climate and craft can transform a familiar variety into something entirely new”.

Ryan explained that he will guide guests through the stories behind each wine, sharing the observations and contrasts that have made Italian varieties such an exciting part of Australia’s contemporary wine conversation.

“Italy is home to hundreds of native grape varieties, and a number of them have found a second home in Australia over recent decades. Regions, like our very own McLaren Vale have become known for growing classic Italian varieties such as Sangiovese, Fiano and Vermentino, while cooler areas like the Adelaide Hills are experimenting with grapes like Nebbiolo. It’s this delicious conversation that La Grande Tavola sets out to explore.

“A single grape variety can tell a completely different story depending on where it’s grown. Place an Italian wine beside its Australian counterpart and you can taste the climate, the soil and the hand of the maker. That’s where the magic is,” he said.

Burnside Village Centre general manager Jodie Kannane said the event reflects the centre’s commitment to delivering premium food, wine and lifestyle experiences in the Village.

“La Grande Tavola is an invitation to slow down, take a seat and experience food and wine in a way that feels personal and beautifully considered.

“With Nick’s extensive knowledge and Eccoci’s modern approach to Italian dining, guests can expect an evening that feels distinctly Burnside Village – refined and memorable,” she said.

The event will take place from 6:30 pm to 9 pm, with tickets priced at $220. More information and bookings are available here.

content:
The Clare Valley Wine & Grape Association (CVWGA) has announced its intention to establish a new national wine competition dedicated exclusively to Riesling, with the inaugural Australian Riesling Challenge proposed for 2027.

As the recognised ‘home of Australian Riesling’, the Clare Valley has played a defining role in building the reputation of the variety over generations. The CVWGA says the proposed competition represents the next step in that legacy, celebrating excellence in Australian Riesling while creating a national platform for producers from every Riesling-producing region.

CVWGA chair Olivia Hoffmann-Barry said the association believes the Clare Valley is uniquely positioned to lead such an initiative.

“For decades, the Clare Valley has been synonymous with Australian Riesling. Our region has helped shape the reputation of the variety, both here and internationally, and we believe it is fitting that the Clare Valley provides a national stage to celebrate the country’s finest Rieslings.”

“This is not about one region. It’s about recognising and promoting the exceptional quality and diversity of Australian Riesling wherever it is grown, while acknowledging the Clare Valley’s long-standing leadership in the category.”

CVWGA wine show subcommittee chair Jarrad Steele acknowledged the significant contribution made by the Canberra International Riesling Challenge, which recently concluded after more than two decades.

“The Canberra International Riesling Challenge played an important role in championing Riesling and recognising excellence across Australia and beyond for many years. The Australian Riesling Challenge is not intended to replicate that event, but rather to build on its legacy with a fresh national platform to focus solely on Australia’s outstanding Riesling producers.”

“As a region renowned for the variety, the Clare Valley has a responsibility to continue leading conversations about the variety and investing in initiatives that strengthen its future. We see this as an opportunity to unite the Australian Riesling community and further elevate the reputation of this remarkable wine style.”

The Australian Riesling Challenge is envisioned as more than a traditional wine competition. The concept aims to bring together judging, education, trade engagement, media exposure and consumer experiences to elevate the profile of Australian Riesling and reinforce its place among the world’s great wine styles.

CVWGA executive officer Cherry Stowman said planning for the competition was underway, with the association working to develop an event worthy of becoming the national benchmark for Riesling.

“The Clare Valley has long championed Australian Riesling, and we see this as a natural evolution of that leadership,” Stowman said.

“Our vision is to create a competition that every Australian Riesling producer wants to win, one that not only recognises excellence, but also generates national conversation, strengthens the category and showcases the diversity of Australia’s Riesling regions.”

The concept will continue to be refined in consultation with the CVWGA board, and winemakers’ committees, with further details regarding the competition format and inaugural event to be announced later this year following completion of the planning process.

The Australian Riesling Challenge is intended to become an annual event hosted in the Clare Valley, reinforcing the region’s position as the home of Australian Riesling, while celebrating the wines and producers that continue to shape the future of the variety across Australia.

content:
South Australian Premier Peter Malinauskas has met with key representatives of the state’s wine industry to hear directly about the challenges facing growers and winemakers and discuss ways to strengthen the future of the industry.

Across the state and the nation, the sector is facing significant pressure from global oversupply, declining grape prices, changing demand and ongoing impacts from previous international trade disruptions.

Premier Malinauskas convened yesterday’s forum with winegrape growers, producers and broader industry representatives, including peak bodies South Australian Wine Industry Association (SAWIA) and Wine Grape Council of South Australia (WGCSA).

“At a time of global oversupply and other challenges facing our wine industry, it’s important that we hear directly from those impacted to learn how we can best support them,” the Premier said.

The South Australian wine sector is a key contributor to the state’s economy, driving trade, jobs and region growth.

“We want to safeguard the future of the state’s wine industry and support South Australian wine grape growers and producers,” said Premier Malinauskas.

The state’s sector produces 80 per cent of Australia’s premium wine and 50 per cent of all bottled wine.

“South Australia produces more than 80 per cent of the nation’s premium wine, from some of the oldest vines in the world, and 50 per cent of all bottled wine,” said SA Minister for Primary Industries and Regional Development, Clare Scriven.

In the 12 months to March 2026, wine was South Australia’s third largest export commodity by value. In that same year, the state exported 317.5 million litres of wine, amounting to $1.62 billion.

South Australia has 680 wineries, 3143 vineyard owners, and 73,156 hectares of vineyards.

The forum aimed to give industry direct access to relevant ministers and agency representatives, to ensure a whole-of-government response to these challenges.

“The aim of bringing these key representatives together is to discuss solutions and impactful ways the State Government can support our industry through these challenges – and make it even stronger,” said Premier Malinauskas.

Minister Scriven reaffirmed the state government’s commitment to the grape and wine sector.

“The Malinauskas Government is committed to supporting our wine industry and [the forum was] an important opportunity to speak directly with growers and wine makers about the challenges they are facing.”

The SA Government announced in June an expanded wine industry development fund to carve out new opportunities for the state’s premium wine regions.

The state government is investing $1.8 million over four years to establish Project 450, a South Australian Wine Industry Association (SAWIA) managed support fund that will provide market and industry development initiatives designed to strengthen and grow South Australia’s premium wine regions.

“We want to continue to strengthen South Australia’s wine industry for the future by not only responding to the challenges but also embracing opportunities for growth,” said Minister Scriven.

The project builds on a range of investments being delivered by the state government to support South Australia’s wine producers to diversify and build new trade relationships, including:

  • $3.9 million to target new export opportunities in China, the US, UK and Southeast Asia, through the Global Wine Growth Program;
  • $1.85 million to re-engage South Australian wine businesses with China, helping to repair a disastrous breakdown in trade relations that occurred under the former Federal Coalition and State Liberal governments;
  • $3.1 million to boost domestic demand, build regional capability, and support vineyard waste management, through the South Australian Wine Recovery Program.

During his recent trip to the United States, the Premier last week signed a Memorandum of Understanding with America’s largest wine and liquor retailer – Total Wine & More – to give South Australian wine producers greater access to the US market.

Described as the ‘US equivalent of Dan Murphy’s’, Total Wine & More operates 294 superstores across 30 states and is already one of the largest retail stockists of premium Australian wine in the United States.

The agreement, signed by Premier Malinauskas and Total Wine & More chief executive Ryan Ross in Maryland, will deliver closer collaboration between South Australia and Total Wine & More to grow the presence of premium South Australian wines across the retailer’s national network through joint promotions, trade education, buyer engagement and category development over the next 12 to 18 months.

title: An air of optimism at Wine Eng 2026
summary:
Wine Eng 2026 kicked off yesterday at Lambert Estate Wines in the Barossa Valley, with an air of optimism radiating from exhibitors, presenters and attendees alike. Daily Wine News was in attendance and caught up with exhibitors to hear why attending the event was meaningful for their businesses and the industry overall. Featuring interviews with Paul Baggio of Bucher Vaslin Pacific, John Fois from TDA Pumps, Stuart Cragg of Anton Paar, Frigid Cloud co-founder Patrick Anderson, Rocco Longo of Enartis, Cooper Boydon of Dixon and Chris Hoskin of Tynic Automation.

The post An air of optimism at Wine Eng 2026 appeared first on Winetitles.
content:
By Kyra Trussell

Wine Eng 2026 kicked off yesterday at Lambert Estate Wines in the Barossa Valley, with an air of optimism radiating from exhibitors, presenters and attendees alike.

Daily Wine News was in attendance and caught up with exhibitors to hear why attending the event was meaningful for their businesses and the industry overall.

Paul Baggio represented Bucher Vaslin Pacific, a supplier of presses, harvest reception and sorting systems as well as membrane filtration solutions.

Baggio said the company has been showcasing new technology to the Australian wine industry this year, which “has been received really well”.

Paul Baggio of Bucher Vaslin Pacific.

As for the highlight of attending the event, Baggio cited meeting people face-to-face.

“In a world of email and text, putting names to faces and just meeting your clients is fundamental. I think it’s become more important than it ever was, and that’s what we’re seeing here today. People actually can interact and they just feel like they can ask questions whereas in writing, generally, we don’t get that nuance,” he said.

When asked about the current state of the industry overall, Baggio expressed there have always challenging times.

“There’s certainly questions and there’s a lot of angst, however, I’m nearly 30 years into the industry this year, and I keep sort of saying the same thing all the time to people that the issues I saw in ’97 when I started are similar, but not linear as per what’s occurring…there’s always been challenges.

“The interesting part that is important about the engineering conference is that the solutions have always been from engineered innovation, and that’s been consistent.

“I guess I have always seen and had faith in that with technology and just with adaption and people understanding how to apply that, that the challenges – not all of them, because there are some that are more marketing and customer related – but certainly with some of the big questions regarding sort of labour force, efficiencies in production, energy and conservation, and just the cost of energy, those are all certainly able to be tackled by technology and innovation,” Baggio concluded.

John Fois from TDA Pumps expressed a similar sentiment.

Brenton Brook and John Fois pictured with the RV65, a primary pump-over pump.

“I think from what I can see, especially with my recent trips to the Riverland, the wine industry is suffering at the moment. But like anything, you know, it has a downturn, and it’s only a matter of time before it comes good again. We’re here to support them, we’re here for them, whether times are bad or times are good,” Fois said.

He expressed that, even though the event is a smaller one, the atmosphere and connection it offers is a standout.

“This Wine Engineering Conference is a great event because the most important people in the wine industry attend it.”

Stuart Cragg of Anton Paar, which supplies laboratory and process equipment, said the event can offer information regarding cost saving solutions for wineries.

Neil Manser and Stuart Cragg of Anton Paar.

“I know it’s quite public that the wine industry is struggling at the moment. So, an event like this, when we’re talking about automation, could be a cost saving for the winery. It’s still quite an important event to take place in these struggling times, and maybe you can pick up some savings by changing things you do around the winery,” he offered.

Cragg said the event is significant for the business to attend as they can “get in touch with the process engineers and decision makers about their future plans and looking to automate around the wine”.

Frigid Cloud co-founder Patrick Anderson said events like these are what keep the industry going.

Jassa Amir-Lang, Mark Gerschwitz and Patrick Anderson, on cloud wine at their Frigid Cloud stall.

“A heap of people here and awesome technology, hopefully some clientele as well. I’m surprised how busy it is and everybody’s pretty upbeat about the industry and where it can go,” he shared.

Rocco Longo of Enartis expressed that the event is about connecting with the wine industry as well as showcasing innovation.

Rocco Longo from Enartis pictured in the exhibition hall.

“I think it’s you’ve got to attend these events because it’s just a way to stay in contact with the community all in one place,” he said.

As for how he views the current state of the industry, Longo emphasised that it’s a “case by case” situation.

“Some wineries, I think, they’re doing really tough overall for a number of geopolitical reasons and oversupply…but there’s some really good news for many other small-to-medium wineries.

“You know, Australia produces some of the best wines in the world, its good quality, so I think it will be an easy pickup once everything does settle.”

Dixon was in attendance to showcase its fluid transfer equipment, including hoses, valves, fittings and more.

Cooper Boydon of Dixon said the event is a good opportunity to come and connect with customers in the wine business.

Cooper Boydon and Connor Dodd of Dixon.

“These events are always good. Just getting everyone together…in the same place and have a chat – connect with one another and pump each other up and get each other going,” he said.

Sanjay Savur of Avca Tech, a company working with Hill Smith Family Estates and the AWRI on its CO2 recovery from fermentation technology, the event was about making new connections.

“It’s something new, so finding what the demand is for this sort of technology, and it’s interesting to be able to get different views on it,” he expressed.

For Chris Hoskin of Tynic Automation, a manufacturer and distributor of engineering plastics and conveyor products, it was the business’s first-time attending Wine Eng.

Chris Hoskn and Aaron Chudleigh of Tynic Automation.

He explained that Tynic hoped to bring awareness to the brand and reach a wider market quickly by attending.

“It’s all about networking, and we just can’t afford as a small Australian business, to do door-to-door, we have to come to events like this to meet everybody.”
